Specimens for a Procedural Typography
             The Galactic faces set against their own framework sentences

                                         Flyxion
                                        Independent Researcher
                                   October 2026

                                               Abstract

                             standardgalactic/fonts      This essay sets the faces of the                              repository to work. Every specimen is
       typeset live in the font it describes, using sentences taken from the titles of Flyxion’s other essays,
      and every specimen is paired with a statement about the font files that is either measured or marked
       as an observation, so that what is shown and what is claimed stay apart. The specimens display five
       things: one sentence in nine faces, the difference between stored text and displayed text, composition
       in the Cistercian numeral block, the behaviour of independent sweeps under two schedules of decay,
      and an order effect in which two operations at matched intensity leave the same summary statistics
      and different outlines.

1  Conventions
A font is easy to describe and hard to judge in prose, because the properties that matter, such as rhythm,
texture, and the ease with which a sentence can be followed, appear only when text is set in  it. The
specimens below are therefore not images pasted into a document. They are lines of ordinary text set by
the typesetter in the font files themselves, which means that every character shown is a character the font
actually contains, and a specimen that required a missing character would have shown a gap, which the
build log reports. Where a face lacks a character, the sentence has been chosen or adjusted to avoid it,
and the text says so.
   The sentences are the titles of other essays by Flyxion, among them the phrases “arrival is not acqui-
sition,” “increments are not contributions,” and “retraction is an operation.” They were chosen because
each names a distinction that the specimen next to it can display, and the pairing of a sentence with a face
is an editorial choice made for that reason. It is not a claim that the essays themselves argue from these
fonts. One further sentence, “intensity does not determine state,” belongs to the companion essay on the
repository and states the idea that organizes the later sections: a font produced by a process is not fixed
by the strength of that process alone.
   Measurements come from the font files at the repository snapshot with the commit hash beginning
0d57718, read with FontTools. Advance widths are in font units, and a figure is quoted with its unit-per-
em value where the comparison needs it. The experiment fonts used here are the Cursive Galactic wave
sweep, the Cursive Galactic full-decay sequence, and the shapeform order-effect pairs, and the build file
expects the repository layout so that it can be compiled with XeLaTeX from the repository root.

                                       1

State

   Set side by side, the faces divide by what they do to an unchanged Latin string. SGA Regular, Systada,
and Dactyl draw the Latin positions as Galactic letterforms, so the stored sentence is ordinary English and
only its appearance has changed, and at this size the three look much alike. Cursive Galactic does the same
with a leaning, more continuous stroke. NovaMono is the opposite case, since it draws the same Latin
string as Latin, in a monospaced face, and keeps its Galactic repertoire elsewhere in the character map.
Logico_philosophicus turns the sentence into an arrangement of signs that resemble notation, Cheiro and
Clypto keep it recognizably English handwriting with different temperaments, and shapeform reduces
each letter to a dark silhouette that no reader could decode without a key, which is why its line is set
word by word with the spacing supplied by the page, the face having no space glyph.
   The resemblance of Systada and Dactyl to SGA Regular at this scale should not be taken to extend
to their spacing. In Systada the hand-drawn Latin letters have advance widths running from 27 to 87
units in a 160-unit em, which makes them proportional, while 542 of the file’s 667 mapped glyphs share
a single advance of 80 units, a half-em cell. Dactyl has the same arrangement with 544 glyphs on the
                                                         FONTLOG.txt80-unit cell and Latin letters between 29 and 92 units. The repository’s                 consists of the
single line “Terminal Friendly Standard Galactic Font,” and on Flyxion’s account it describes Systada. The
measurements are compatible with that purpose in one respect only: the borrowed glyphs that make up
most of the map sit on a uniform cell, as a terminal expects, but the hand-drawn Latin letters do not, so
a line of Systada text will not align in columns the way a monospaced face does. The comparison in the
terminal section below makes that visible.

3  Stored text and displayed text
The same sentence can reach the page by three routes, and the faces show the differences directly. In
the first the stored characters are Latin and the font changes their appearance. In the second the stored
characters are private-use code points from the registry block for Standard Galactic, so that the identity
of the script is part of the stored text. In the third a font such as NovaMono draws its Latin positions as
Latin and reserves the private-use positions for the Galactic letters, so that a single file can display both
a plain string and a Galactic string without any change of font.
Stored as Latin: “Arrival is not acquisition. in SGA Regular
Arrival is not acquisition.

Stored as Latin: the same string in NovaMono, drawn as Latin
Arrival is not acquisition.

Stored as private-use code points: SGA Regular

   The private-use string is what a registry-aware document would store. Its letters are the code points
U+EB40       U+EB59        through          in alphabetical order, so that the letter a is U+EB40, the letter i is U+EB48, the
letter l is U+EB4B, the letter r is U+EB51, and the letter v is U+EB55, and the full stop is U+EB5F. Spaces
are ordinary spaces. The three faces draw the string in three manners. SGA Regular and Cursive Galactic
both build the private-use letters from pixel-like blocks, and although the outlines of all twenty-six letters
differ between the two files, the rows look alike at this size, the Cursive row being slanted slightly. That
is worth noting because Cursive Galactic’s Latin-position forms are the flowing ones, so the face keeps its
cursive manner for the stored-Latin route and a blocky manner for the registry route. NovaMono draws
the same letters with thinner strokes in its wider monospaced cells. The three agree on which letter each
code point means, and that agreement is the practical content of a shared registry, since text stored this
way keeps its script identity when it moves from one of these fonts to another. The Latin-position string,
by contrast, would look like English to any font that did not know the convention, and it would have lost
nothing in storage.
   The NovaMono pair is the cleanest demonstration, because one file draws the two stored strings in two
different ways. The comparison also bears on the earlier remark that a screenshot cannot say what was
typed, what was stored, and what was drawn. These specimens answer all three questions only because
the stored strings are given alongside them.
   The block also contains its own boundary markers. In SGA Regular and Cursive Galactic the three
       U+EB5Apositions         to U+EB5C, which the registry proposal leaves unassigned, are filled with labelled boxes
                                                            U+EB5D    U+EB5Ethat show the hexadecimal address, followed by the two quotation marks at        and        and
the full stop at U+EB5F. NovaMono fills the same six positions with much smaller marks in place of the
labelled boxes.

4  Composition in the Cistercian block
The Cistercian numeral block shows composition rather than substitution. Under the registry proposal
                  U+EBA0   U+EBA9the units digits occupy         to        and are ordinary spacing characters, while the tens, hundreds,
                      U+EBB1         U+EBC1             U+EBD1and thousands digits occupy         to U+EBB9,         to U+EBC9, and         to U+EBD9, are marked
as combining, and have no zero. In SGA Regular every units digit advances the cursor by 1,024 units,
and every higher-place digit has an advance of zero, so that its outline overlays the character before it. A
numeral is therefore stored as a short sequence and displayed as one sign.
2026 as three characters: units 6 (EBA6), tens 2 (EBB2), thousands 2 (EBD2); no hundreds digit because the hundreds place
is zero
                                  

1234 as four characters: units 4 (EBA4), tens 3 (EBB3), hundreds 2 (EBC2), thousands 1 (EBD1)
                                              
                                       5

The three faces draw the same assembled sign in three hands, which confirms that the overlay works
across files and is a property of the convention and of the font metrics, not of one design. It also shows
why placeholders must be read locally. The unused positions in this block, among them the zero positions
                      U+EBAAof the combining ranges and         to U+EBAF, are not missing numerals, because the proposal assigns
nothing there.

5  The terminal comparison
Three faces are set below with the same short shell lines taken from the repository’s own instructions,
followed by a test string that exposes whether a face keeps its letters on a grid. A monospaced face sets
every character on the same advance, so a row of narrow letters and a row of wide letters end in the same
place.
NovaMono Standard Galactic (monospaced Latin)
$ python make_experiments.py
$ python make-experiment-index.py
$ python -m http.server

   In NovaMono the three test rows have the same length, as the advance widths require, since all ninety-
four printable ASCII characters in the file have one advance of 1,150 units in a 2,048-unit em. In Systada
and Dactyl the rows differ in length, because the Latin letters carry their own widths. The terminal-
friendly face in this collection is therefore NovaMono for Latin reading and, for Galactic reading, a face
whose uniform cell covers its borrowed glyphs and not its letters. A reader who wanted Galactic text on
a strict character grid would need the private-use letters or a modified face, and the repository does not
yet say which of its files is meant for that.

6  Two sweeps from one source
The sequence fonts in the repository were produced by a function that takes the original font, applies the
transformation at one parameter value, and saves the result, for each value in turn. Each state is therefore
a function of its own parameter and of the source, and no state is built from another. The wave sweep
for Cursive Galactic runs from amplitude 0 to amplitude 120 in eight steps at a fixed frequency of 2.0, so
that the integer amplitudes are 0, 17, 34, 51, 68, 85, 102, and 120. The full-decay sequence stacks three
operators, jitter, baseline droop, and stroke collapse, whose strengths all rise together, reaching at the last
step a jitter of 40, a droop of 0.6, and a collapse of 0.5. The lines below set one sentence through each
state.

   Reading down either block gives an impression of progressive damage, although the change between
neighbouring states is slight at reading size and the difference across the whole range is clearer than any
single step. That impression is the point of the next observation. The progression is real as an ordering of
parameters, but it lives in the way the states are arranged and in the reader’s passage down the page. It is
not stored in any one font, since state 005 contains no trace of state 004. The sweep is a good instrument
for asking how recognition depends on the strength of a distortion at a given moment, and it is a poor
instrument for asking whether the order of earlier exposures alters later ones, because the files cannot
carry that order.

7  One document under two schedules
The repository separates the schedule by which a document moves through the states from the states
themselves. A small module maps a position in the document, from zero at the first sentence to one at the
last, to an intensity, with linear, quadratic, cubic, smoothstep, and cliff shapes, and the document generator
uses such an intensity to choose a font. The two paragraphs below contain the same eight sentences and
the same eight wave-sweep fonts. The first reads them under the linear schedule and the second under
the cliff schedule with the module’s default parameters, a cliff at 0.7 and a floor of 0.15. Each intensity
is mapped to the nearest of the eight states, which is a convention adopted for this specimen. The states
used by the linear paragraph are 000, 001, 002, 003, 004, 005, 006, 007, and those used by the cliff
paragraph are 000, 000, 000, 001, 001, 001, 004, 007.
linear schedule

Familiarity with a script is cumulative. A reader arrives at a skill by a

path. Two readers at one level need not share that path. A degraded font

                                       9

is also the product of a path. A sweep builds every state from the source.

A cumulative sequence builds each state from the last.  The order of

operations can change the outline. The intensity alone does not say which.

cliff schedule

Familiarity with a script is cumulative. A reader arrives at a skill by a

path. Two readers at one level need not share that path. A degraded font

is also the product of a path. A sweep builds every state from the source.

A cumulative sequence builds each state from the last.  The order of

operations can change the outline. The intensity alone does not say which.

   Both paragraphs begin in the clean source and end in the heaviest state, so a comparison of endpoints
would find them identical. What differs is the amount of the document spent near each level of distortion.
The linear paragraph passes steadily through every state, while the cliff paragraph spends its first six
sentences in the two states closest to the source and then falls quickly through a middle state to the last.
A reader following the second paragraph meets a different experience of the same sentences even though
the same eight fonts have been used, which is the sense in which the nominal endpoints of a degradation
do not fix what a reader encounters on the way.

8  An order effect in matched fonts
The v02 experiments include a pair of sequences made from shapeform, one that applies a wave and then
a grid quantization at each of five intensities and one that applies the grid first and the wave second. The
pair is the repository’s direct demonstration that the order of two operations can matter. The lines below
set one phrase in the two orders at three of the five states, and shapeform’s silhouettes should be read as
shapes, since the face encodes its letters as dark forms that are not meant to be decoded by eye.
state 000, wave then grid
Retraction Is An Operation

state 000, grid then wave
Retraction Is An Operation



                                      10

state 002, wave then grid
Retraction Is An Operation

state 002, grid then wave
Retraction Is An Operation

state 004, wave then grid
Retraction Is An Operation

state 004, grid then wave
Retraction Is An Operation

   The recorded measurements for the fourth state show how little the repository’s own summary statis-
tics can say about the difference. Both outputs have the same 682 points in the same 58 contours, and
their total contour lengths are 88,329.059 units for wave then grid and 88,105.381 units for grid then
wave, a gap of about a quarter of one percent, against a source length of 82,475.39. Their bounding boxes
                                                       −36differ by only a few units at the top, at 828 against 844, and at the bottom, at      against −50. The
two fonts nonetheless differ point by point. Comparing corresponding points across the 682 in the two
fourth-state fonts gives a mean displacement of 14.8 units, with a largest displacement of 44.0, while each
differs from the source by a mean of about 60 units, with a largest displacement of about 107. At state
002 the mean displacement between the two orders is 6.8 units with a maximum of 21.0, and at state
000 the two are identical, with a displacement of 0.0, although each is about 0.9 units from the source on
average. The order effect is therefore small beside the effect of the operations themselves and invisible to
the recorded summary statistics, yet it is measurable in the outlines. This is the repository’s own caution
made concrete, that its geometric records do not settle perceptual questions, and it supplies a matched
pair on which a reader experiment could test whether a difference of this size matters to recognition.

9  Faces with narrow inputs
Three faces ask for a specific kind of input and show their behaviour only when they receive it. Cheiro
and Clypto contain letters and a few punctuation marks, and neither contains digits, the hyphen, or
parentheses, so the sentence below has been set without its hyphen.
Cheiro, with the hyphen omitted because the face has none
Task sufficient preservation.

Clypto, with the hyphen omitted because the face has none
Task sufficient preservation.

   Logico_philosophicus lacks only the underscore among the printable ASCII characters, so it accepts
the full sentence together with digits and punctuation, and the result shows prose acquiring the look of
formal notation while remaining ordinary text at the level of the stored characters.
Logico_philosophicus, with digits and punctuation
Task-sufficient preservation. 0123456789 (a, b; c: d).

mathematical monospace block. It is meant to receive a sequence already converted by the cipher tool, so

   Shown this way the face is a set of twenty-nine carriers whose conventional identities, a mathematical
sign or a syllabic character, are unrelated to the letters they stand for in the cipher. Software that does
not know the convention treats them as what they are, which is why a screenshot of this face establishes
neither the original text nor the stored characters.

10  What the specimens add
The specimens turn several statements that were made abstractly in the companion essay into things that
can be looked at. The difference between a glyph count and a character count appears as the difference
between a Latin string and a private-use string drawn in one face. The claim that a numeral can be stored
as several characters and displayed as one appears as a composite sign in three hands. The distinction
between an independent sweep and a cumulative sequence appears as a block of states that look like
progress and contain no history, and the effect of a schedule appears as two paragraphs with the same

                                      12

endpoints and different journeys. The order effect appears as a pair of fonts whose recorded summaries
nearly coincide and whose outlines do not.
   They also mark what remains untested. None of the specimens measures how well anyone reads any
of them. The sweeps and schedules are arranged for a reader, but no reader has been timed, and the
order-effect pair is ready for a recognition test that has not been run. The terminal-friendly claim has
been narrowed by measurement to the borrowed glyphs of Systada, with NovaMono the only face here
that keeps Latin letters on a grid. The set of faces has been shown to share a registry convention for
Standard Galactic letters across three files, and not across all ten.
                              specimens.tex   To reproduce the specimens, place                   in the root of the repository, with the font files
and the experiment directories named in the preamble in their usual places, and compile it twice with
XeLaTeX. The preamble loads Amiri from the repository for the running text, so no font outside the
repository is needed.
